entities.title: Britain and Ireland
entities.description: Explore selected archaeological evidence from Britain and Ireland alongside the wider world.
entities.note: 500–251 BCE is an editorial research window, not the start or end of these places. Coverage is partial; the examples below do not represent every community.

entities.title: Danebury
entities.description: A hillfort in Hampshire with evidence of houses, food storage and crafts.
entities.note: The study range follows an older 550–100 BCE chronology; another account dates construction around 470 BCE. Start dates remain disputed. The map marks the site, not a territory.

entities.title: Life at Danebury
entities.description: Archaeology reveals roundhouses, grain storage and craft activities at this Hampshire hillfort.
entities.note: Broad site history, not year-by-year activity. Construction is variously dated around 550 or 470 BCE; individual buildings and activities need phase-specific dating.

entities.title: Broxmouth’s changing settlement
entities.description: A Scottish settlement changed between enclosed and unenclosed forms over a long Iron Age sequence.
entities.note: Modelled start: 640–570 BCE; abandonment: 155–210 CE, each at 68% probability. The band uses the outer limits of those estimates, not exact dates or a confidence interval for every year. No precise map point is included yet.

entities.title: Ireland’s Iron Age landscape
entities.description: Older monuments were reused during Ireland’s Iron Age.
entities.note: Broad context for the source’s conventional 500 BCE–400 CE period. It does not establish the date of each reuse, or what happened specifically in 399 BCE.

entities.title: Castell Henllys
entities.description: A Pembrokeshire hillfort with evidence of farming and metalworking.
entities.note: Reported start estimates span about 410–375 BCE and end estimates about 380–190 BCE. The outer plotted range is not proof of occupation in every year. In 399 BCE the overlap is possible, not certain.

entities.title: The Castell Henllys community
entities.description: A Pembrokeshire hillfort with evidence of farming and metalworking.
entities.note: Reported start estimates span about 410–375 BCE and end estimates about 380–190 BCE. The outer plotted range is not proof of occupation in every year. In 399 BCE the overlap is possible, not certain.

entities.title: Wheeled transport at Doogarrymore
entities.description: Two wooden cart wheels found with a trackway provide evidence of wheeled transport in County Roscommon.
entities.note: The museum guide dates the cart’s use to the fourth century BCE. This is dating uncertainty, not evidence of continuous use for a century, and does not establish use in 399 BCE. No precise findspot is mapped yet.

entities.title: Corlea
entities.description: An Irish bogland site where an oak-plank roadway was built in the second century BCE.
entities.note: This view concerns Corlea 1, one of several trackways. The construction estimate is 148–147 BCE, not a two-year duration. The marker is the excavation report’s site reference, not a route outline.

entities.title: Building the Corlea roadway
entities.description: An oak-plank roadway was built at Corlea; its construction is dated to 148–147 BCE.
entities.note: A single construction year within this two-year estimate. It is centuries later than Socrates. Its precise purpose remains uncertain.

entities.title: Predynastic Egypt
entities.description: Nile Valley communities developed distinct regional cultures before Egyptian political unification.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Badarian communities
entities.description: The ministry places Badarian culture around 5500–4000 BCE near modern Asyut.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Maadi cultural complex
entities.description: The Maadi cultural complex developed near modern Cairo around 4000–3100 BCE.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Naqada I communities
entities.description: The ministry describes increasing social differentiation towards the period’s end.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Egypt’s Old Kingdom
entities.description: Much of the surviving evidence for material culture comes from funerary contexts.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Djoser’s reign and Step Pyramid
entities.description: His Saqqara funerary complex included Egypt’s first pyramid.
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan or precise construction interval. Chronologies vary; this follows the Met.

entities.title: Khufu and the Great Pyramid
entities.description:
Khufu ruled Egypt during the Fourth Dynasty, succeeding his father Snefru. His tomb, the Great Pyramid at Giza, is the largest pyramid in Egypt.

His father had already commissioned three enormous pyramids and developed their smooth-sided form. Khufu’s pyramid continued that work, as part of a complex with temples, a causeway and nearby cemeteries for officials.

Power was concentrated around the king, with senior offices often held by his relatives. The state planned the cemeteries around Khufu’s pyramid too, placing officials close to the king in death.
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan or precise construction interval. This follows the Met’s chronology.

entities.title: Egypt’s New Kingdom
entities.description: A settlement in western Thebes housed artists who made royal tombs.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Urban life at Uruk
entities.description: Clay pictographs recorded goods and workers’ rations, preceding later cuneiform.
entities.note: 3200–3000 BCE is an editorial window around the source’s early urban context, not the lifespan of Uruk. The city continued afterwards.

entities.title: Mesopotamian city-states
entities.description: City rulers acquired luxury materials through trade and conquest.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Indus urban communities
entities.description: Seals preserve writing that remains undeciphered.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Shang China
entities.description: Its political centre lay along the Yellow River in present-day Henan.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Western Zhou
entities.description: Zhou rulers exercised authority across much of central China.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Eastern Zhou
entities.description: After the capital moved to Luoyang, regional states became increasingly autonomous.
entities.note: Dynastic context overlaps Spring and Autumn and Warring States. Their boundary dates vary between chronologies; this is not an additional separate dynasty.

entities.title: Western Han
entities.description: Chang’an was its capital, with palaces, residential wards and market areas.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Eastern Han
entities.description: Its capital was Luoyang; diplomacy and long-distance exchange expanded.
entities.note: Shown through 220 CE to preserve the source’s full period, slightly beyond the initial 200 CE collection scope. The gap after Western Han is intentional.

entities.title: Emperor Wu’s reign
entities.description: His reign promoted Confucian learning in official conduct and education.
entities.note: These are reign dates, not the emperor’s lifespan.

entities.title: Olmec Gulf Coast communities
entities.description: Sculptors used imported volcanic stone and jade.
entities.note: Approximate, source-specific period boundaries. This is a broad introduction, not a year-by-year account. Map location is not yet researched.

entities.title: Monumental La Venta
entities.description: Monumental building and carving there ceased after about 400 BCE.
entities.note: Approximate overview of monumental activity, not the dates of every building or all occupation.

entities.title: Caral and the Supe Valley
entities.description: Its architecture includes large platform mounds and sunken circular courts.
entities.note: Broad archaeological context. The map marker is UNESCO’s site reference, not a territorial boundary.

entities.title: Kush and the Meroe region
entities.description: The Meroe region preserves royal, religious, domestic and water-management remains.
entities.note: Broad regional context across many phases. Dates represent whole centuries and do not date each monument. This extends beyond 200 CE for context; borders and year-specific locations remain unresearched.

entities.title: Ancient world overview
entities.description: Compare selected histories across Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas.
entities.note: An editorial browsing window, 3000 BCE–200 CE. Use Fit study period to see the whole range; selecting this area preserves your current dates. Predynastic context extends earlier. This is a growing sample, not complete world coverage.

entities.title: Jōmon communities in northern Japan
entities.description: Settled communities relied on hunting, fishing and gathering; their sites preserve dwellings, graves, earthworks and stone circles.
entities.note: Regional archaeological context for southern Hokkaido and northern Tohoku. Dates do not apply uniformly to all Japan or every settlement. The full sequence begins before the initial study window. No single map point represents these scattered sites.

entities.title: Life at Sannai Maruyama
entities.description: At Aomori, planned dwellings, storage pits and roads accompanied a diet evidenced by nuts, fish and animal remains; imported materials included jade and obsidian.
entities.note: Whole-site dates are used. The guide separately labels Stage IIb as 3000–2200 BCE. Archaeological remains span phases; a precise map reference has not yet been checked.

entities.title: Korean dolmen communities
entities.description: These cemeteries preserve hundreds of tombs assembled from large stone slabs.
entities.note: 1000–1 BCE represents the source’s whole-millennium dating, not continuous construction or the date of any individual tomb. Three separated site groups are not represented by a single point.

entities.title: Dilmun’s burial landscapes
entities.description: Bahrain’s role as a trading centre supported elaborate burial traditions, preserved in extensive mound fields and royal tombs.
entities.note: Dates describe this group of burial monuments, not the entire history of Dilmun. The property has 21 component sites; their individual map references remain to be checked.

entities.title: Lapita settlement and pottery
entities.description: Communities expanded eastward across the western Pacific and made distinctively decorated pottery.
entities.note: Broad source-specific chronology. Islands were settled at different times; this band is not an annual migration route or territorial boundary. Geographic associations need further research.

entities.title: Arnhem Land’s X-ray rock art
entities.description: Artists depicted internal organs and bones within human and animal figures.
entities.note: The timeline is clipped at 200 CE to fit this collection’s study window; this is not the end of a continuing Aboriginal artistic tradition. Dates are approximate and do not date every painting. No single map point is assigned.

entities.title: Chavín’s ceremonial landscape
entities.description: Its place of worship includes terraces, plazas and dressed-stone structures with animal-like ornament.
entities.note: These are broad cultural dates, not construction dates for every monument. The marker is the archaeological site reference, not the extent of Chavín influence.

entities.title: Poverty Point’s mound builders
entities.description: Hunter-fisher-gatherers built monumental earthworks in the Lower Mississippi Valley and participated in far-reaching exchange networks.
entities.note: This follows the NPS World Heritage article’s date range, not a date for each mound. UNESCO’s BP wording has not been converted into calendar years. The marker locates the site, not its trading network.

entities.title: Sammallahdenmäki’s burial cairns
entities.description: Communities built granite burial cairns in clusters along a ridge in western Finland.
entities.note: This is a Bronze Age context band, not the full lifespan of the cemetery. UNESCO also records two excavated cairns from the Early Iron Age. The site marker is not a cultural boundary.

entities.title: Teotihuacán’s monumental city
entities.description: Large pyramids and temples formed part of a city laid out according to geometric and symbolic principles.
entities.note: The full source period extends beyond 200 CE. Monuments belong to different phases; this does not imply all were present in the first century or that settlement began in 1 CE. The map marker locates the archaeological site.

entities.title: Villanovan communities
entities.description: The Met places Villanovan culture approximately between 900 and 500 BCE and identifies it as a predecessor of Etruscan culture.
entities.note: Approximate archaeological chronology, overlapping the emergence of Etruscan culture. These are not two successive states with a sharp boundary; map locations remain unresearched.

entities.title: Etruscan cities and crafts
entities.description: Metal-rich Etruria supported skilled bronze workers whose products circulated around the Mediterranean.
entities.note: Broad cultural context, not the lifetime of a unified state or every Etruscan city. The end is a rounded century boundary from the source. No historical territory is reconstructed.

entities.title: The Parthian Empire
entities.description: Trade supported patronage of sculpture, metalwork, jewellery and ceramics, combining Hellenistic and earlier Near Eastern traditions.
entities.note: A broad imperial period, extending slightly beyond 200 CE. Artistic practices and frontiers changed over time; no fixed border or year-specific capital location is implied.

entities.title: Mithridates I’s reign
entities.description: The Met gives Mithridates I’s reign as approximately 171–138 BCE.
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. The source describes expansion under this ruler and his successors collectively; individual campaigns are not dated here.

entities.title: Early settlement at Jenne-jeno
entities.description: The settlement occupied the fertile Middle Niger floodplain in what is now Mali.
entities.note: An editorial early-history window ending at 200 CE, not the end of settlement. The source continues to about 1400 CE; its later urban walls, professional districts and medieval empires are not assigned to this early window. Precise site coordinates remain unverified.

entities.title: Aksum and Red Sea exchange
entities.description: Its exchange networks linked inland northeastern Africa with the Red Sea through the port of Adulis.
entities.note: Broad kingdom context with the full source period retained beyond 200 CE. Famous stelae date mainly to the third and fourth centuries and are not presented as first-century monuments. The marker locates Aksum, not Adulis or the kingdom’s borders.

entities.title: Early Buddhist Sanchi
entities.description: Ashoka’s pillar and a brick stupa were followed by enlargement and ornamentation under later dynasties.
entities.note: An early sanctuary phase, not the full duration of Sanchi. Buildings and additions belong to different dates; the site continued long after 100 CE. The marker is UNESCO’s archaeological site reference.

entities.title: Scythian communities around the Black Sea
entities.description: Politically diverse pastoral horse-riding communities traded and interacted with neighbouring Greek settlements.
entities.note: 750–100 BCE is a rounded editorial envelope for the source’s late-century boundaries. It is not a precise migration date or the end of all Scythian communities. A mobile, diverse population is not represented by one point or a single state border.

entities.title: Early Dynastic Egypt
entities.description: The first two dynasties followed the formation of a united Egyptian kingdom.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened.

entities.title: Egypt’s First Intermediate Period
entities.description: Provincial governors gained independence as central royal control weakened.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened.

entities.title: Egypt’s Middle Kingdom
entities.description: Royal reunification was followed by construction, trade, agricultural projects and literary innovation.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened.

entities.title: Egypt’s Second Intermediate Period
entities.description: Hyksos power in the northeastern Delta coexisted with Egyptian rulers farther south.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened.

entities.title: Egypt’s Third Intermediate Period
entities.description: Kings based at Tanis shared power with increasingly autonomous authorities in Upper Egypt.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened.

entities.title: Egypt’s Late Period
entities.description: Kushite, Saite and Persian phases form part of this broad period of changing rule.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened. The source heading begins in 747 BCE, while its prose also uses the narrower Saite starting point of 664 BCE.

entities.title: Macedonian and Ptolemaic Egypt
entities.description: Alexander’s conquest was followed by rule under Ptolemy and his successors.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened. The 332 BCE start includes Macedonian rule before Ptolemy became king.

entities.title: Egypt under Roman rule
entities.description: Egypt became a Roman province; agriculture and production served the imperial economy.
entities.note: Approximate period boundaries follow the Egyptian ministry. Other entries use museum chronologies, so boundaries can overlap or leave small gaps; these are dating differences, not evidence that nothing happened. The full source period extends beyond the initial 200 CE study window.

entities.title: Snefru’s reign
entities.description: Snefru: approximately 2575–2551 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Khafre’s reign
entities.description: Khafre: approximately 2520–2494 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Menkaure’s reign
entities.description: Menkaure: approximately 2490–2472 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Amenemhat I’s reign
entities.description: Amenemhat I: approximately 1981–1952 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Senwosret III’s reign
entities.description: Senwosret III: approximately 1878–1840 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Hatshepsut’s reign
entities.description: Hatshepsut: approximately 1473–1458 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty. This records kingship, following an earlier regency (1479–1473 BCE in the source).

entities.title: Thutmose III’s reign
entities.description: Thutmose III: approximately 1479–1425 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Amenhotep III’s reign
entities.description: Amenhotep III: approximately 1390–1352 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Akhenaten’s reign
entities.description: Akhenaten: approximately 1349–1336 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty. The Met separates his earlier name Amenhotep IV (1353–1349 BCE); this entry shows the Akhenaten phase only.

entities.title: Tutankhamun’s reign
entities.description: Tutankhamun: approximately 1336–1327 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Seti I’s reign
entities.description: Seti I: approximately 1294–1279 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Ramesses II’s reign
entities.description: Ramesses II: approximately 1279–1213 BCE (Met reign chronology).
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Memphis
entities.description: The city was an important centre for the worship of Ptah.
entities.note: Editorial browsing window 3100 BCE–200 CE, not the city’s complete lifespan. The traditional foundation story is not treated as a precisely dated event. The map uses UNESCO’s Site of Memphis reference, not a city boundary.

entities.title: Thebes (Egypt)
entities.description: Thebes was a capital in the Middle and New Kingdoms and a major centre of Amun worship.
entities.note: Editorial browsing window from the Middle Kingdom through 200 CE; neither the city’s founding nor its abandonment. The map uses the Karnak component as a reference within a city with multiple temples and necropolises; it is not a city centre or boundary. This is Egyptian Thebes, distinct from the Greek city.

entities.title: Akhenaten’s religious changes
entities.description: The king promoted Aten worship and founded a new capital, Akhetaten, in Middle Egypt.
entities.note: Reign-sized context, not an exact date for every reform or the founding of the city. This ministry chronology differs slightly from the Met’s name-specific reign entries.

entities.title: The royal tomb workers of Deir el-Medina
entities.description: At Deir el-Medina in western Thebes, a community of artists and craftspeople created royal tombs and left evidence of everyday life.
entities.note: Shown within broad New Kingdom context from the source, not as exact settlement foundation and abandonment dates. A site-specific map reference has not yet been checked.

entities.title: Djedefre’s reign
entities.description: Djedefre ruled after Khufu and before Khafre, during Egypt’s Fourth Dynasty. The Met dates his reign to approximately 2528–2520 BCE.
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Approximate chronology follows the Met; overlaps can reflect co-rule or chronological uncertainty.

entities.title: Egypt’s Fourth Dynasty
entities.description:
The Fourth Dynasty includes the reigns of Snefru, Khufu, Djedefre, Khafre and Menkaure. The Met places it at approximately 2575–2465 BCE, within the Old Kingdom.

Use the connected reigns to explore individual rulers, or keep this wider view to compare their period with events elsewhere.
entities.note: Approximate dynasty boundaries follow the Met’s chronology. Connected reigns are a selection, not a complete king list.

entities.title: Stonehenge
entities.description:
Stonehenge developed over many generations. The first earthwork was built around 3000 BCE; the main stone settings followed around 2500 BCE.

The early monument was also a burial place. Later changes included rearranging the bluestones and creating the Avenue towards the River Avon. The date range here covers its principal prehistoric building phases, not its entire history.
entities.note: Approximate construction dates, not exact years. The overall study window does not imply continuous work or abandonment in 1500 BCE.

entities.title: Stonehenge’s first earthwork
entities.description: Around 3000 BCE, people built a circular ditch and banks at Stonehenge. Cremated remains were buried within and around the monument.
entities.note: Approximate construction dates, not exact years. The overall study window does not imply continuous work or abandonment in 1500 BCE.

entities.title: Raising Stonehenge’s stones
entities.description: Around 2500 BCE, builders erected the large sarsens and smaller bluestones at the centre of Stonehenge.
entities.note: Approximate construction dates, not exact years. The overall study window does not imply continuous work or abandonment in 1500 BCE.

entities.title: Stonehenge’s later changes
entities.description: Bluestones were rearranged and the Avenue was built around 2300–2200 BCE. The Y and Z pits date to around 1800–1500 BCE. These were separate episodes, not continuous building work.
entities.note: Approximate construction dates, not exact years. The overall study window does not imply continuous work or abandonment in 1500 BCE.

entities.title: Ubaid villages and towns
entities.description:
Ubaid communities farmed with irrigation and fished the rivers and Gulf. Between about 5500 and 4000 BCE, related pottery traditions spread across much of Mesopotamia.

Some villages grew into towns centred on large buildings, including at Eridu and Uruk. These developments preceded the better-known cities of the Uruk period.
entities.note: The displayed span follows the Met’s period of widespread Ubaid culture. Its southern origins are earlier, around 6200 BCE.

entities.title: Mesopotamia’s Uruk period
entities.description:
During the Uruk period, cities developed around large mud-brick temples. The Met places this period at approximately 4000–3100 BCE.

Growing administration changed how goods and transactions were recorded. Clay tablets and cylinder seals became part of this changing urban society. The separate Uruk city entry lets you explore the later part of this period more closely.
entities.note: Approximate regional chronology, not the lifespan of a single city. Administrative changes developed within the period, not all at its beginning.

entities.title: Building Avebury
entities.description:
Avebury’s banks, ditches and stone circles were built and altered over centuries, roughly between 2850 and 2200 BCE. It was a ceremonial complex rather than a single construction project.

The order in which its features appeared is still being investigated. That matters when comparing Avebury with Stonehenge: both changed over time, and their surviving forms combine different stages.
entities.note: Approximate construction and alteration window. The precise sequence remains uncertain.

entities.title: Village life at Skara Brae
entities.description:
Skara Brae was a village in Orkney occupied around 3100–2500 BCE. Its stone houses preserve details of domestic life, including hearths, beds and storage furniture.

People farmed, hunted and fished, and made pottery, tools and jewellery. The surviving rooms bring ordinary households into view alongside the monuments and royal tombs elsewhere on the timeline.
entities.note: Approximate occupation dates follow Historic Scotland’s management plan. The reason village life ended is uncertain.

entities.title: Building Newgrange and the Boyne tombs
entities.description:
Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth were built around 3200 BCE in the Boyne Valley in Ireland. These passage tombs form part of the wider Brú na Bóinne landscape.

Their carved stones preserve a substantial collection of megalithic art. The date shown marks their approximate construction, not the end of their use or significance.
entities.note: A rounded construction date for several monuments, not a claim that they were all built in one year.

entities.title: Yangshao communities
entities.description:
Yangshao communities belong to Neolithic China, approximately 5000–3000 BCE. Their surviving objects include painted pottery, stone tools and equipment for working textiles.

The National Museum of China’s collection includes knives, a stone mortar, spindle whorls and bone needles. Together they offer a view of practical work and decorated objects, long before the later dynasties.
entities.note: Broad archaeological culture, not a unified state. Date ranges vary between sites and phases.

entities.title: Liangzhu’s city and waterworks
entities.description:
Liangzhu developed in the lower Yangtze region around 3300–2300 BCE. Rice cultivation supported a society whose remains include a planned city, large earthworks and systems for managing water.

Differences between burials also show differences in status. This gives us another early urban history to place beside Egypt and Mesopotamia, without assuming that their societies followed the same pattern.
entities.note: Dates follow UNESCO’s archaeological site chronology, not every site associated with Liangzhu culture.

entities.title: Malta’s megalithic temples
entities.description:
Communities on Malta and Gozo built substantial stone temples during the fourth and third millennia BCE. The surviving complexes differ in their plans and decoration.

Builders combined upright slabs with horizontal stonework, creating enclosed spaces approached through forecourts. The broad timeline window brings these building traditions into view; it does not date every temple to the same phase.
entities.note: Editorial span covers the fourth and third millennia BCE stated by UNESCO. It is not an exact start or end date for temple construction.

entities.title: Communities before the kingdom of Kerma
entities.description:
Before the kingdom of Kerma, communities along the Nile developed a large enclosed settlement in Upper Nubia. The archaeological mission places this Pre-Kerma phase around 3500–2500 BCE.

The enclosure suggests concern with protecting people and their resources. Evidence from the wider region is limited, so the extent of connections with neighbouring communities is harder to reconstruct.
entities.note: Broad Pre-Kerma phase. The site evidence does not establish a single state throughout Upper Nubia.

entities.title: The kingdom of Kerma
entities.description:
Kerma was the centre of a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, near the Nile’s Third Cataract. Its capital and eastern cemetery preserve evidence spanning roughly 2500–1500 BCE.

These sites provide a history of political power and burial traditions in Nubia itself. Explore the earlier Pre-Kerma communities to see the longer history of settlement in the area.
entities.note: Approximate archaeological chronology of the kingdom’s capital and cemetery.

entities.title: Early cultivation at Kuk
entities.description:
At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people cultivated plants on raised mounds along wetland margins. Research dates this phase to about 5000–4490 BCE and identifies intensive banana cultivation.

The evidence supports an independent origin of agriculture in New Guinea. This was a different setting and farming tradition from those developing around the Nile or in Mesopotamia.
entities.note: Dated evidence for the onset of this cultivation phase, not its full duration. Converted from 6950–6440 calibrated years BP using the conventional 1950 reference year.
entities.dateLabel: Dated evidence · onset of cultivation phase

entities.title: Ditched cultivation at Kuk
entities.description:
Later farmers at Kuk used ditches to cultivate wet ground. The research dates the beginning of this phase to about 2400–2030 BCE.

This follows the much earlier evidence for cultivation on mounds. The two entries separate changes in farming practice rather than treating thousands of years of activity as one event.
entities.note: Dated evidence for the onset of a phase, not a continuous construction programme. Converted from 4350–3980 calibrated years BP using the conventional 1950 reference year.
entities.dateLabel: Dated evidence · onset of cultivation phase

entities.title: Watson Brake’s mound builders
entities.description:
At Watson Brake in present-day Louisiana, people built a complex of eleven earthen mounds and connecting ridges. Construction developed in episodes, beginning with smaller earthworks around 3500 BCE.

Food remains indicate a varied diet including nuts, fish and deer. Large communal earthworks were part of this foraging society, well before the later mound complex at Poverty Point.
entities.note: The displayed 3500–2800 BCE site range follows 64 Parishes. Saunders and colleagues date substantial mound raising from about 3350 BCE until after 3000 BCE; work was episodic.

entities.title: Julius Caesar
entities.description:
Julius Caesar lived from 100 to 44 BCE, during the final decades of the Roman Republic. His rise ended in dictatorship and assassination.

His death did not restore political stability. His heir Octavian, later known as Augustus, eventually emerged as Rome’s first emperor. The connections below follow the people and conflicts that link Caesar’s lifetime to that change.
entities.note: Lifespan, using the conventional birth year of 100 BCE. Some chronologies give 102 BCE; age comparisons here follow 100.

entities.title: Cleopatra VII
entities.description:
Cleopatra VII lived from 69 to 30 BCE and was the last queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty. Her position joined the politics of Egypt to the struggles for power in Rome.

Her relationships with Caesar and then Mark Antony were also political alliances. In Egypt, she drew on established traditions of royal authority while adapting them to her own circumstances.
entities.note: Lifespan. Her reign is a separate entry, beginning in 51 BCE.

entities.title: Pompey
entities.description:
Pompey lived from 106 to 48 BCE. He first worked with Caesar in a political alliance, then fought against him in civil war.

Defeat at Pharsalus drove him to Egypt, where he was killed.
entities.note: Lifespan. The map does not imply that he remained in Rome throughout it.

entities.title: Cicero
entities.description:
Cicero was a Roman politician, lawyer and philosophical writer. His speeches and letters give us a particularly close view of the Republic’s final decades.

As consul in 63 BCE, he suppressed Catiline’s conspiracy. He later watched the struggle between Caesar and Pompey turn into civil war. Caesar’s assassination brought only a brief respite: Cicero was killed on Mark Antony’s orders in 43 BCE.
entities.note: Lifespan, 106–43 BCE.

entities.title: Mark Antony
entities.description:
Mark Antony fought for Caesar and became one of the central figures in the struggle after his death. He and Octavian were allies before becoming rivals.

His alliance with Cleopatra tied his future to Ptolemaic Egypt. Octavian defeated their forces at Actium in 31 BCE. Antony died the following year.
entities.note: Lifespan, using 83–30 BCE. Regional labels describe his wider career, not a continuous location.

entities.title: Augustus (Octavian)
entities.description:
Born in 63 BCE, Octavian became Caesar’s heir after the assassination in 44 BCE. He was still a young man when he entered the struggle for power that followed.

Victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium removed his principal rivals. In 27 BCE, the Senate granted him the title Augustus. He died in 14 CE; his lifespan and his years as emperor are shown separately.
entities.note: Lifespan. Octavian and Augustus are the same person; Augustus is the title granted in 27 BCE.

entities.title: Cleopatra’s reign
entities.description:
Cleopatra ruled Egypt from 51 to 30 BCE. She belonged to the dynasty established by Ptolemy I, one of Alexander’s successors.

Her reign brought that long history into direct contact with Caesar, Antony and Octavian. The links here lead back into Ptolemaic Egypt and forward to Roman rule.
entities.note: Reign dates, not a lifespan. Co-rulers and interruptions are not yet represented as separate phases.

entities.title: Caesar becomes consul
entities.description:
Caesar became consul in 59 BCE with the support of Pompey and Crassus.

The alliance helped secure his command in Gaul after his year in office.
entities.note: First consulship; Caesar held the office again later.

entities.title: Caesar’s campaigns in Gaul
entities.description:
Caesar campaigned in Gaul from 58 to 50 BCE. During these years, his armies also crossed the Channel into Britain.

The two British expeditions belong within this wider series of campaigns. They did not establish lasting Roman occupation of Britain.
entities.note: Campaign window follows English Heritage. It includes the closing phase after the principal conquest; fighting was not continuous everywhere.

entities.title: Caesar’s expeditions to Britain
entities.description:
Caesar crossed to Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE. The second expedition was the larger attack, directed against communities in the south-east.

His troops withdrew. Diplomatic and trading relationships continued across the Channel, but permanent Roman occupation came much later.
entities.note: Two separate expeditions, not two years of continuous occupation.

entities.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
entities.description:
In 49 BCE, Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy.

This crossing began open civil war with Pompey and his allies.
entities.note: Year-level event; the marker does not specify a disputed crossing site.

entities.title: The battle of Pharsalus
entities.description:
Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in 48 BCE.

Pompey escaped to Egypt. Caesar followed, bringing the Roman conflict into the struggle over Egypt’s throne.
entities.note: Battle year. This was not the end of the civil war.

entities.title: Caesar and Cleopatra in Alexandria
entities.description:
Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BCE and supported Cleopatra’s claim to the throne.

Fighting kept him in Egypt into 47 BCE. He left Cleopatra in power, supported by Roman troops.
entities.note: Episode spanning parts of 48 and 47 BCE, not two complete years. The map uses Egypt’s existing regional reference, not a palace location.

entities.title: The assassination of Caesar
entities.description:
Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE. His concentration of power had made the survival of republican government a central issue.

His death opened another struggle for control. Octavian, his heir, eventually became Augustus.
entities.note: 15 March 44 BCE, displayed at year resolution.

entities.title: The battle of Actium
entities.description:
On 2 September 31 BCE, Octavian defeated the forces of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium.

Follow their connections to see how this Roman conflict also became the final crisis of Ptolemaic Egypt.
entities.note: Battle date, displayed at year resolution. Egypt’s annexation followed in 30 BCE.

entities.title: Egypt comes under Roman rule
entities.description:
Roman rule began in Egypt in 30 BCE, after Cleopatra’s death. The Ptolemaic dynasty, established by Ptolemy I in 305 BCE, had ended.

This is the point where the Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt entries meet. It marks a change in government, not an end to Egyptian society or its traditions.
entities.note: Political transition in 30 BCE. The wider Roman Egypt entry covers the subsequent period.

entities.title: The reign of Augustus
entities.description:
In 27 BCE, the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus. This entry follows his rule from that settlement to his death in 14 CE.

His separate life entry begins in 63 BCE, allowing you to compare his age with Caesar, Cleopatra and Antony.
entities.note: Conventional imperial reign, 27 BCE–14 CE. His rise to sole power began before the title was granted.

entities.title: Sanchi’s carved gateways
entities.description:
In the first century BCE, elaborate stone gateways were added to the Great Stupa at Sanchi. The Archaeological Survey of India associates this work with the Andhra-Satavahanas.

The carvings tell stories from the Buddha’s life and the Jatakas. Alongside the wars around the Mediterranean, the timeline shows a community investing in a Buddhist sanctuary with a much longer history.
entities.note: First-century BCE construction window, not continuous work over a hundred years. Individual gateways are not dated separately here.

entities.title: Alcibiades
entities.description:
Alcibiades was an Athenian politician and commander whose career crossed the divisions of the Peloponnesian War. Brought up under Pericles’ guardianship, he became closely associated with Socrates.

He helped persuade Athens to send its great expedition to Sicily, then fled to Sparta after being recalled for trial. His later return to Athenian service makes his life a useful way through the war’s changing alliances.
entities.note: Approximate lifespan: sources give 451/450–404/403 BCE. The timeline uses 450–404, so age comparisons are approximate.

entities.title: Pericles
entities.description:
Pericles was an Athenian politician and commander, born around 495 BCE. His career belonged to the period when Athens became a dominant power in the Greek world.

He was still leading the city at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the epidemic in 429 BCE, early in a conflict that would continue for another quarter of a century.
entities.note: Approximate birth year; lifespan, not a reign. Athens was a democracy, and Pericles was not its monarch.

entities.title: Nicias
entities.description:
Nicias was an Athenian commander and politician who favoured peace with Sparta. The treaty negotiated in 421 BCE bears his name.

He opposed the proposed expedition to Sicily but nevertheless became one of its commanders alongside Alcibiades and Lamachus. His career ended with the expedition’s defeat in 413 BCE.
entities.note: Born around 470 BCE; died in 413 BCE. The opening decades of his life are poorly documented.

entities.title: Sparta
entities.description:
Sparta led the coalition fighting Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Its victory in 404 BCE forced Athens to give up its empire.

Alcibiades’ connection takes you inside that rivalry: after leaving Athenian service, he sought refuge with the Spartans and advised them against his own city.
entities.note: 450–404 BCE is this entry’s study window, not the founding or end of Sparta. The point locates the city, not Spartan territory. Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory.

entities.title: Syracuse
entities.description:
Syracuse was the principal target of the Athenian expedition to Sicily. Its defenders, aided by the Spartan commander Gylippus, resisted the siege.

The Athenian expedition was destroyed in 413 BCE. Syracuse’s connections show this part of the war from the city being attacked, rather than only from Athens.
entities.note: 415–413 BCE is an editorial campaign window, not the lifespan of the city. The marker uses Ortygia’s UNESCO reference point. UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position.

entities.title: The Peloponnesian War
entities.description:
The Peloponnesian War set Athens and its allies against Sparta and its coalition. It ran from 431 to 404 BCE, with a negotiated peace interrupting the main conflict.

Fighting extended well beyond the two cities. The Sicilian expedition and Persian involvement are part of the same history. Athens eventually surrendered and lost its empire.
entities.note: Overall war chronology. This span does not mean uninterrupted fighting in every region.

entities.title: The epidemic at Athens
entities.description:
A severe epidemic struck Athens during the early years of the war. People had crowded into the city for protection, and the disease killed soldiers and civilians, including Pericles in 429 BCE.

Thucydides survived it and described what he saw. The illness is conventionally called the plague of Athens, but its precise cause remains uncertain.
entities.note: Outbreaks between 430 and 426 BCE, not a claim of constant intensity. No modern diagnosis is presented as settled. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Socrates and Alcibiades at Potidaea
entities.description:
Socrates and Alcibiades were deployed to Potidaea in 432 BCE. Socrates served as a hoplite, an infantry soldier.

The episode places their relationship in military service as well as philosophical conversation.
entities.note: Deployment year. The campaign and siege continued afterwards; this entry does not date every episode associated with them.

entities.title: The battle of Delium
entities.description:
Socrates fought at Delium in 424 BCE, when the Athenian army was defeated.

Plato’s dialogues later present Alcibiades and Laches praising his conduct during the retreat. These are literary accounts of the event, not transcripts made on the battlefield.
entities.note: Battle year; testimony about Socrates is identified as coming through Plato.

entities.title: The Peace of Nicias
entities.description:
Athens and Sparta agreed to peace in 421 BCE after ten years of war. Nicias was closely associated with the negotiations.

The settlement did not resolve the rivalries between the cities and their allies. The later Sicilian expedition and renewed war show how limited the peace proved.
entities.note: Treaty concluded in March 421 BCE; not the final end of the Peloponnesian War.

entities.title: The Sicilian expedition
entities.description:
Athens sent a major expedition to Sicily in 415 BCE. Alcibiades, Nicias and Lamachus shared the initial command.

Alcibiades was recalled, and the remaining commanders pursued the campaign against Syracuse. Despite reinforcements, the expedition ended in disaster in 413 BCE. Many survivors became prisoners.
entities.note: Campaign dates. The Syracuse marker represents a principal target, not every landing or battle in Sicily. UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position.

entities.title: The mutilation of the herms
entities.description:
Just before the fleet sailed for Sicily, sacred stone figures called herms were mutilated across Athens. The attack provoked an investigation into sacrilege.

Alcibiades became caught up in accusations concerning religious offences. Accusations against him should not be read as proof that he personally damaged the herms.
entities.note: 415 BCE. The herm mutilations and accusations concerning the Mysteries were connected investigations, not identical charges. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Alcibiades turns to Sparta
entities.description:
Recalled from Sicily for trial in 415 BCE, Alcibiades escaped to Sparta. He advised Athens’ enemies as the war widened.

By 412 BCE he was helping Spartan operations in Ionia. This was a changing political allegiance, not an uninterrupted stay in the city of Sparta.
entities.note: Broad phase of Spartan cooperation, 415–412 BCE. The city marker indicates his refuge, not his location in every year. Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory.

entities.title: The coup of the Four Hundred
entities.description:
An oligarchic coup replaced Athenian democracy with the government of the Four Hundred in 411 BCE. Hopes of obtaining Persian support formed part of the political manoeuvring.

Alcibiades was involved in proposals linking a change of government to his own return. The new regime was divided from the start.
entities.note: Coup year. The Four Hundred were a different regime from the Thirty of 404 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Alcibiades returns to Athens
entities.description:
Alcibiades returned to Athens in 407 BCE after years away from the city.

His return belongs to the war’s final phase. It did not end the conflict, which continued until Athens’ defeat in 404 BCE.
entities.note: Return to the city, distinct from his earlier return to command of Athenian forces. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The generals’ trial after Arginusae
entities.description:
After the naval victory at Arginusae in 406 BCE, Athens prosecuted the commanders over the failure to recover men and bodies from the sea.

Socrates opposed the unlawful collective proceedings. Six generals were executed.
entities.note: Trial in Athens, not a marker for the battle at sea. This is distinct from Socrates’ own trial in 399 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The battle of Aegospotami
entities.description:
Lysander defeated the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE.

The defeat was followed by the siege of Athens. The city surrendered the following year.
entities.note: Naval defeat in 405 BCE. No precise battlefield coordinates are asserted.

entities.title: Athens surrenders to Sparta
entities.description:
Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, ending the Peloponnesian War. Its Long Walls were demolished.

Peace did not immediately restore political stability. The government of the Thirty and a civil conflict followed.
entities.note: Surrender in spring 404 BCE, displayed at year resolution. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The Thirty rule Athens
entities.description:
After Athens’ defeat, an oligarchic government known as the Thirty took power with Spartan backing. Opposition to its rule developed into civil war.

The regime was short-lived. Democratic forces recovered ground, and a settlement in 403 BCE restored democracy.
entities.note: Government of 404–403 BCE, not a lifespan. Its aftermath provides context for Socrates’ later trial without claiming a single cause for his prosecution. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: Democracy returns to Athens
entities.description:
A settlement in 403 BCE restored Athenian democracy after the rule of the Thirty and the fighting that followed. The Spartan king Pausanias intervened in the reconciliation.

Socrates’ trial belongs to this restored democracy, four years later. The two events should not be collapsed into one.
entities.note: Restoration in 403 BCE. Socrates’ separate trial entry is dated 399 BCE. Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location.

entities.title: The reign of Darius II
entities.description:
Darius II ruled the Persian Empire during the later years of the Peloponnesian War. His officials negotiated with Sparta, and Persian money helped support its fleet.

This places the war within a wider struggle over influence in the Aegean and western Anatolia. Persia was an active participant, not just a distant background.
entities.note: Reign, not lifespan. The displayed 423–404 BCE follows Livius; the accession falls across 424/423 BCE.

entities.title: Amyrtaeus challenges Persian rule in Egypt
entities.description:
Around 404 BCE, Amyrtaeus established himself as an Egyptian ruler and began consolidating independence from Persia. He was the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty.

The change did not happen everywhere at once. Documents from Elephantine still recognised the Persian king as late as 401 BCE. This is a gradual political transition, despite the single date on the timeline.
entities.note: Approximate accession date, not the instant liberation of all Egypt. The end of his reign is outside this entry’s scope.

entities.title: The Mauryan Empire
entities.description:
The Mauryan dynasty brought much of the Indian subcontinent under one ruling house. Chandragupta founded it, followed by Bindusara and Ashoka.

Its capital was Pataliputra. The connections here follow the rulers, their dealings with Alexander’s successors and the surviving evidence of Ashoka’s reign.
entities.note: Approximate dynastic chronology follows the Met’s main text, 321–185 BCE; its heading uses 323. No fixed territorial border is implied.

entities.title: Chandragupta Maurya’s reign
entities.description:
Chandragupta took power in Magadha and established the Mauryan dynasty. His expansion connected the Ganges valley with the north-west, where Alexander’s successors were competing for control.

He reached a settlement with Seleucus. Bindusara succeeded him; the date of that succession is approximate.
entities.note: Reign, not lifespan. Uses Livius’s conventional 321–c.297 BCE chronology. Early Mauryan chronology is debated.

entities.title: Bindusara’s reign
entities.description:
Bindusara succeeded his father Chandragupta and was followed by his son Ashoka. His reign sits between two better documented rulers.

Accounts attribute expansion in central India to him, but some assign the same conquests to Ashoka. The division is uncertain.
entities.note: Approximate reign, not lifespan, following Livius. Other chronologies place the succession to Ashoka differently.

entities.title: Ashoka’s reign
entities.description:
Ashoka was the third Mauryan emperor. He supported Buddhism and had inscriptions placed across his empire.

These surviving texts make his rule unusually visible. They let us compare what a king said about government and conduct with the monuments and places connected to his reign.
entities.note: Reign, not lifespan. The Met uses c.273–232 BCE; Livius gives accession in 272. Accession and coronation chronologies differ. No birth date is inferred.

entities.title: Ashoka’s rock and pillar inscriptions
entities.description:
Ashoka used inscriptions on rock and polished stone pillars to communicate beyond his court. They recorded royal instructions and ideas about conduct.

The surviving inscriptions are evidence of particular statements in particular places, rather than proof that every subject lived by the same rules.
entities.note: Editorial window from the Met’s starting date of 254 BCE to the end of Ashoka’s reign. Not a continuous carving programme or the date of every edict.

entities.title: Seleucus I Nicator
entities.description:
Seleucus served under Alexander and later established a kingdom of his own. He sought refuge with Ptolemy in Egypt before recovering power in Babylonia.

His settlement with Chandragupta connects the struggles among Alexander’s successors with the rise of the Mauryan state. He was assassinated in 281 BCE.
entities.note: Approximate birth c.358 BCE; death 281 BCE. Lifespan, not reign. No continuous personal itinerary is inferred.

entities.title: Chandragupta and Seleucus make peace
entities.description:
Chandragupta and Seleucus reached a settlement after conflict near the Indus. Their agreement connected the Mauryan state with one of the kingdoms formed after Alexander’s death.

The early evidence does not clearly establish who won the fighting. Later accounts have turned that uncertainty into very different stories.
entities.note: One episode within approximately 305–303 BCE, following Jansari’s publisher synopsis. This range does not establish three years of uninterrupted warfare or a precise treaty date.

entities.title: Pataliputra under the Mauryas
entities.description:
Pataliputra was the Mauryan capital. The Greek envoy Megasthenes described a city defended by a timber wall, gates and towers.

That account gives us a view of the capital through a visitor’s writing. It should not be treated as a complete description of everyday life there.
entities.note: Editorial window follows the dynasty, not the foundation or end of the city. Megasthenes’ description is literary testimony. The map uses Kumrahar’s archaeological site reference within Pataliputra, not the city’s centre or extent. The identification as Ashoka’s palace is not treated as certain.

entities.title: Lumbini
entities.description:
Lumbini is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in what is now southern Nepal. Its archaeological remains include Ashoka’s inscribed pillar and structures dating back to the third century BCE.

The pillar connects the place to a recorded royal visit, alongside the longer history of worship at the site.
entities.note: Third-century BCE study window, not the lifespan of the site. UNESCO’s traditional date for the Buddha’s birth is not used here. The point is the World Heritage property reference.

entities.title: Ashoka’s visit to Lumbini
entities.description:
Ashoka visited Lumbini and erected an inscribed pillar there. UNESCO dates the pillar to 249 BCE.

This is a dated connection between a ruler and a place, rather than a general assumption that he visited every site associated with his dynasty.
entities.note: Year follows UNESCO. The map uses the property reference, not a reconstructed route.

entities.title: Taxila
entities.description:
Taxila preserves several successive settlements. The Bhir mound contains the remains of an early historic town; Sirkap and Sirsukh belong to later phases.

Its position brought it into contact with Persia, the Greek world and Central Asia. Buddhist monasteries and monuments were part of its changing urban landscape.
entities.note: 500 BCE–200 CE is an editorial window within a much longer history. The point marks Bhir Mound, one component of the UNESCO property, not all Taxila or a political border.

entities.title: Alexander enters Taxila
entities.description:
Alexander entered Taxila in 326 BCE. UNESCO associates this episode with the Bhir mound, the earliest historic settlement in the archaeological complex.

The city’s history extends beyond that encounter. Its other entries and connections put the campaign alongside the region’s urban and religious history.
entities.note: Year follows UNESCO. The point is the Bhir Mound site reference, not an exact camp or route.

entities.title: Qin Shi Huang
entities.description:
Ying Zheng conquered the remaining rival states and became the First Emperor. His government imposed common systems of writing, money and measurement.

His burial complex, with its terracotta army, gives a different view of the resources his rule could command.
entities.note: Lifespan follows the Met. The point associated with his death is his tomb, not a location for every year of his life.

entities.title: The Qin Empire
entities.description:
Qin’s conquests brought the competing states under one emperor. Officials administered the new empire through commanderies and prefectures.

The dynasty was short-lived, but its administrative arrangements influenced later governments.
entities.note: Dynastic period, distinct from the earlier state of Qin. No fixed territorial outline is implied.

entities.title: Qin unifies the competing states
entities.description:
In 221 BCE, Qin’s conquests established a unified empire under the First Emperor.

This marks a change in government across the conquered states, rather than the beginning of Chinese history.
entities.note: Year follows UNESCO. Unification refers to the contemporary competing states, not the borders of modern China.

entities.title: The First Emperor’s mausoleum
entities.description:
Work on the First Emperor’s burial complex began in 246 BCE. Its layout echoed the capital, Xianyang.

The tomb mound, surrounding pits and terracotta army formed parts of a much larger funerary landscape near present-day Xi’an.
entities.note: Construction study window ends with the emperor’s death. It does not date every feature or imply the site ceased to exist.

entities.title: Making the terracotta army
entities.description:
The First Emperor’s burial complex contained thousands of clay soldiers and horses, alongside weapons and bronze chariots.

Their surviving details provide evidence of military equipment and the work of potters and metalworkers.
entities.note: Broad mausoleum construction window, not independently established start and finish dates for the statues. The point marks the army pits.

entities.title: Chang’an under the Western Han
entities.description:
Chang’an was the Western Han capital. Palaces, residential districts and markets occupied a city organised along a north–south axis.

It provides an urban setting for the dynasty’s rulers, writers and trade.
entities.note: Western Han study window, not foundation dates or an assertion that it was the capital from the first year. The map uses UNESCO’s Weiyang Palace site reference within Han Chang’an, not the later Tang capital or a city boundary.

entities.title: Sima Qian’s Historical Records
entities.description:
Sima Qian’s Shiji became a model for later Chinese histories. It also described peoples beyond the empire’s borders.

Those descriptions preserve the historian’s perspective as well as information about the people he discussed.
entities.note: Editorial window uses Emperor Wu’s reign. These are not the start and completion dates of the work or Sima Qian’s lifespan.

entities.title: Ban Chao
entities.description:
Ban Chao was a Han general from a literary family. Between 73 and 94 CE he reasserted Han control in Central Asia.

His career connects the Eastern Han with the routes and communities to its west.
entities.note: Lifespan follows the Met. The campaign range does not supply a year-by-year itinerary.

entities.title: Luoyang under the Eastern Han
entities.description:
The Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang, east of the earlier capital at Chang’an. Two large palace complexes dominated the city.

Caravans and visiting envoys connected the capital with places beyond the empire.
entities.note: Eastern Han study window, not the foundation or end of the city. The map uses UNESCO’s Eastern Han–Northern Wei city site reference, not the later Sui–Tang city or a historical boundary.

entities.title: Octavia the Younger
entities.description:
Octavia was Augustus’ sister and married Mark Antony. She tried to mediate between the two men as their alliance deteriorated.

After Antony’s death, she brought up children from his marriages and his relationship with Cleopatra alongside her own family. Her household became part of the dynasty Augustus was building.
entities.note: Approximate lifespan. The plotted dates follow Livius’s 69 BCE birth and use 11 BCE from its alternative death dates of 11 or 10 BCE.

entities.title: Livia Drusilla
entities.description:
Livia married the future Augustus in 38 BCE and became an important adviser. Her son Tiberius eventually succeeded him.

She continued to exercise influence after Augustus’ death. Hostile stories about her role in the family’s deaths should not be treated as established fact.
entities.note: Lifespan follows Store norske leksikon: 58 BCE–29 CE. Dates are at year resolution; there is no year zero. No continuous personal location is inferred.

entities.title: Ban Zhao
entities.description:
Ban Zhao was a scholar and teacher at the Eastern Han court. She helped complete the history of the Western Han after her brother Ban Gu died.

Her writing also addressed women’s education and conduct. It gives us a named woman’s argument about family life, rather than a neutral account of how every household worked.
entities.note: Approximate lifespan follows Columbia: c.48–c.116 CE. Pang-White’s Cambridge summary gives c.45–117. These are uncertain endpoints, not exact ages.

entities.title: Octavia brings support to Athens
entities.description:
Plutarch describes Octavia arriving in Athens with money, clothing and soldiers for Antony. He told her to remain there.

This records a particular journey in the breakdown of their marriage and political alliance. It does not provide a complete itinerary.
entities.note: The Loeb edition’s footnote dates the arrival to 35 BCE. The map uses the Acropolis to locate Athens, not to claim that Octavia visited that monument.

entities.title: Livia marries the future Augustus
entities.description:
Livia married Octavian, the future Augustus, in 38 BCE after her divorce from Tiberius Claudius Nero.

Their marriage joined the family of her sons Tiberius and Drusus with the man who would become Rome’s first emperor.
entities.note: Year follows Store norske leksikon. No wedding location is assigned.

entities.title: Ban Zhao’s Lessons for Women
entities.description:
Ban Zhao’s Lessons for Women discussed education, marriage and conduct. It combined an argument for women’s learning with expectations of obedience within the household.

Read as advice, the text reveals the standards its author wanted women to follow. It cannot tell us how all women actually lived.
entities.note: Approximately 100 CE, following Pang-White’s public chapter summary. The single plotted year is an approximate date, not an exact publication year.
